> Why It's a Problem:
> 
> 1. The  tag is inline by default, and putting a block-level element like  inside it was not allowed in older HTML specs.

This is not an actual problem, this is just a piece of history.

> 
> 2. HTML5 relaxed the rules slightly (e.g., allowing block-level content if  wraps flow content), but many linters, screen readers, and accessibility tools still flag this as bad practice.

These are bugs in those tools, which you should file on those tools, not the spec.

> 
> 3. It is better to use a  or wrap only inline/phrasing content, or apply styling differently.

This appears to be an opinion, and not an actual problem.

Hi @domenic Hope you are fine.

Thanks for the clarification. While HTML5 permits this, in practice, nesting block-level elements inside <a> causes real issues with accessibility, maintainability, and tooling. I believe it’s important to highlight this as a pragmatic problem, even if not a spec violation. Encouraging better best practices benefits the developer community.


But emphasize practical experience:
From a frontend developer and accessibility standpoint, it causes headaches. It’s better practice to avoid it for maintainability and accessibility reasons.

Raise the issue with linters and accessibility tools:
Since those tools flag it, report these warnings as intentional, not bugs, or at least ask for better explanations.

Document it as a best practice in your team/projects:
Even if spec allows it, enforce a rule like:

Do not put  <div>  inside  <a>   to keep code semantic, accessible, and easier to maintain.

> ### What problem are you trying to solve?
> Placing block-level elements like
> 
> inside an tag violates HTML5 semantic rules and can lead to accessibility issues, inconsistent rendering across browsers, and problems with validation tools.
> Why It's a Problem:
> 
> 1. The  tag is inline by default, and putting a block-level element like  inside it was not allowed in older HTML specs.
> 2. HTML5 relaxed the rules slightly (e.g., allowing block-level content if  wraps flow content), but many linters, screen readers, and accessibility tools still flag this as bad practice.
> 3. It is better to use a  or wrap only inline/phrasing content, or apply styling differently.
> 
> Bad Example (Violates Semantics):
> 
> Click Here
> Good Example (Semantically Correct): [ Click Here ](https://example.com)
> 
> Or, using a block element styled like a link:
> 
> Click Here
> ### What solutions exist today?
> 1. Use inline elements like  inside
> 
> If you want to wrap part of the text or add styling, use inline elements instead of
> 
> .
> html: [ Click here ](https://example.com)
> 
> css: .highlight { font-weight: bold; color: blue; }
> 
> 2. Use a  or block element as a link with ARIA role and keyboard support
>    If you need a whole block clickable but can’t use  with block inside, use a  and add accessibility:
> 
> html:
> 
> Click here (block div acting like a link)
> * role="link" tells screen readers this behaves like a link.
> * tabindex="0" makes it focusable via keyboard.
> * The onkeypress handles Enter key activation.
> 
> ### How would you solve it?
> Avoid nesting block-level elements inside .
> 
> If styling or layout requires, wrap inline elements () inside .
> 
> Only use ARIA role and keyboard handlers on non- elements when absolutely necessary.
> 
> ### Anything else?
> * Accessibility matters: Using semantic tags properly helps screen readers and keyboard users.
> * SEO matters: Search engines expect links inside  tags.
> * Avoid unexpected behavior: Nesting block elements inside inline ones can cause browser quirks.
> * Use linting tools: Configure ESLint/HTMLHint to warn about block elements inside .
> 
> Analogy: Kitchen Items in Bedroom (Explaining
> 
> Inside )
> If it’s your own home, it’s okay to keep kitchen items in the bedroom because you know where everything is.
> But:
> * It’s not a good way to maintain your home.
> * It doesn't look organized or standard.
> * If a new person or guest visits, they’ll get confused searching for things.
> 
> Similarly, putting a
> 
> inside an tag is allowed by browsers, but:
> * It’s bad for maintainability and semantic clarity.
> * It breaks expected HTML structure standards.
> * It causes confusion for new developers, screen readers, and tools that expect cleaner code.
> 
> This analogy helps explain why something might be technically possible but still discouraged for better code quality and future-proofing.
